assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Neutron star
items.clue: The extremely dense remnant left at the centre after a supernova.

items.label: Red super giant
items.clue: The stage a star much more massive than the Sun swells into when it leaves the main sequence.

items.label: White dwarf
items.clue: The small, dense remnant left when a red giant of about the Sun's size collapses at the end of its life.

items.label: Artificial satellite
items.clue: A man-made object placed in orbit around a planet, held in that orbit by gravity in the same way as a moon.

questions.stem: What determines the life cycle that a star will follow?

options.text: The colour of the star, which shows its surface state
How bright the star looks when viewed from Earth
The size of the star, which sets the path it takes
The age of the star, since all stars follow one path

questions.explanation: The specification states that the life cycle of a star is determined by the size of the star.

questions.stem: What allows a planet or a satellite to maintain a circular orbit?

options.text: Gravity provides the force that keeps it in its circular orbit
There is no gravity in space, so it just keeps drifting round
Its engines fire all the time to hold it in its orbital path
An outward force balances gravity and holds it in place

questions.explanation: The specification states that gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites, both natural and artificial, to maintain their circular orbits.

questions.stem: A star about the size of the Sun leaves the main sequence. What happens next?

options.text: It explodes straight away as a supernova
It shrinks back to become a protostar
It becomes a white dwarf at once
It expands and becomes a red giant

questions.explanation: For a star of about the Sun's size, the stage after the main sequence is the red giant.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares moons and artificial satellites?

options.text: Both orbit a planet, but only the moon is held there by gravity
Both orbit a planet; moons are natural and satellites are man-made
Both orbit the Sun directly, and both were formed with the Sun
Neither one is held by gravity, since gravity does not act in space

questions.explanation: Moons and artificial satellites both orbit a planet and are both held in orbit by gravity. The distinction is that moons are natural and satellites are made by people.

questions.stem: What is the full sequence of stages at the end of the life of a star about the size of the Sun?

options.text: Red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf
Red giant, then supernova, then a neutron star
Red super giant, then supernova, then black hole
White dwarf, then red giant, then a black dwarf

questions.explanation: A star of about the Sun's size swells into a red giant, collapses to a white dwarf, and finally cools to a black dwarf.

questions.stem: What happens to a star much more massive than the Sun after the main sequence?

options.text: Red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf, just as the Sun will
Red super giant, then supernova, then neutron star or black hole
Red super giant, then supernova, then always a black hole
Red super giant, then protostar, then a new main sequence star

questions.explanation: A star much more massive than the Sun becomes a red super giant, explodes as a supernova, and leaves a neutron star or a black hole.

questions.stem: What can be left at the centre after a massive star explodes as a supernova?

options.text: A black hole, whatever the mass of the star that exploded
A white dwarf that later cools to become a black dwarf
A neutron star, or a black hole if the star was massive enough
Nothing at all, as the star is completely destroyed

questions.explanation: A supernova leaves a very dense neutron star, and for the most massive stars a black hole.

questions.stem: Which elements are produced by fusion processes in stars?

options.text: Only hydrogen and helium, and nothing more
Only those elements that are heavier than iron
All of the naturally occurring elements
Only elements made by the splitting of nuclei

questions.explanation: The specification states that fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements.

questions.stem: Where are the elements heavier than iron produced?

options.text: In the explosion of a massive star, a supernova
In the fusion reactions inside a main sequence star
Nowhere; they have existed from the very start
By the splitting of very large nuclei inside the star

questions.explanation: The specification states that elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova.

questions.stem: What does the explosion of a massive star do to the elements it has produced?

options.text: It leaves the elements locked inside the remnant star
It distributes the elements throughout the whole universe
It destroys the elements, leaving only hydrogen gas
It converts all the elements into ones lighter than iron

questions.explanation: The specification states that the explosion of a massive star (supernova) distributes the elements throughout the universe.

questions.stem: How do fusion processes in stars lead to the formation of new elements?

options.text: Large nuclei split apart to form smaller nuclei of new elements
Atoms join chemically to make new compounds and elements
Fusion makes only the elements heavier than iron in the core
Small nuclei join to form larger nuclei of different elements

questions.explanation: In fusion, small nuclei join to form a larger nucleus. Because the number of protons changes, the new nucleus is a nucleus of a different element.

questions.stem: (HT only) A satellite travels round a circular orbit at a steady rate. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Its speed and its velocity are both remaining constant
Its speed keeps increasing because gravity acts upon it
Its speed stays the same but its velocity is changing
Its velocity is constant but its speed is changing

questions.explanation: In a circular orbit gravity acts at right angles to the motion, so it changes the direction of travel and therefore the velocity, while the speed is unchanged.

questions.stem: (HT only) A satellite in a stable circular orbit is made to travel faster. For the orbit to stay stable, what must happen?

options.text: The radius of the orbit must become much larger
The radius of the orbit can stay exactly as before
The orbit turns into a straight line at once
The radius of the orbit must get smaller

questions.explanation: For a stable orbit the radius must change if the speed changes: a faster orbital speed corresponds to a smaller orbital radius.
